pr_title: Delay writing a terminal phase until the pod is terminated
pr_body:
Other components must know when the Kubelet has released critical resources for terminal pods. Do not set the phase in the apiserver to terminal until all containers are stopped and cannot restart.  Because the pod worker was inferring the transition to terminal state due to the propagation of the phase to the API and then back in from the config loop (which means that if the apiserver is down, failed and succeeded pods aren't torn down on the node), we need to instead have syncPod signal that the normal lifecycle of the pod has led to termination.

After those two changes, one of the init container tests was failing because TerminatePod was defaulting regular container status to the unknown error (137) even though we know for sure in this case no regular containers were ever started.  Correct TerminatePod defaulting to only include plausibly started containers (according to the pod lifecycle).  It's possible that the race that led to pods succeeding even though we never successfully ran the necessary containers is now fixed, but a future change will have to experiment with that.

Fixes #106884, #108733

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/kind regression

```release-note
Fixed a 1.22 regression that could incorrectly reject pods with OutOfCpu errors if they were rapidly scheduled after other pods were reported as complete in the API. The Kubelet now waits to report the phase of a pod as terminal in the API until all running containers are guaranteed to have stopped and no new containers can be started.  Short-lived pods may take slightly longer (~1s) to report Succeeded or Failed after this change.
```

Yeah, that's desirable if this turns out to be the right fix - the status manager needs to be aggressive at flushing the final status and that warning is us trying to avoid duplicate work (although the warning is too chatty if we go down this path).

Directly described the transition from a syncPod where the pod is known terminal into syncTerminatingPod.  That should address the failure to transition described in the previous failures (and is a necessary consequence, since the Kubelet "knows" that we transitioned to terminating, but was instead relying on a status update to propagate it).

The failure in the init container test is a real bug that was masked by phase short circuit.  Looking at it now.

Working through the status behavior in the latest commit, I *think* after the changes to status here, we may no longer need TerminatePod to default the status (the bug that originally led to status being reported was due to this race between pod status and pod phase), but that's a larger change.  Also, #107845 probably has to merge first, because failures in CRI could hold it.

The change to leave the container in waiting is intentional - the pod is failed (initialization didn't succeed), the container could *never* have been started (initialization didn't pass).  So that is a deliberate consequence of my change - we shouldn't say the regular container exited if it cannot be proven to have started (we have no evidence it started, which means at the time the pod failed the container was 'waiting').

We have had a lot of bugs because containers that never really terminated were listed as accidentally exitCode=0 (the default), which accidentally led to succeeded pods (that didn't clearly succeed).  I think of this change as "we can't set `terminated != nil` unless we actually observed a start, or we can't prove we didn't start it at some point and then lost the status".

The test change in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/108599 can be cherrypicked into this PR as an additional test case to test fix for https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/108594. This was a deliberate design choice - a Kubelet must consider the resources of terminating pods, and a pod that is terminating but not terminal AND pods that are force deleted (not visible in the API) can still be consuming resources (for instance, volumes or reserved CPUs). Previously, in this case we would be allowing our consumption to burst over what the node could support (and exclusive resources might fail to allocate at all).

I agree that this exposes a conflict between scheduler and kubelet, but it's still possible for the kubelet to have more resources committed than can be observed by the system (a force deleted pod still consumes resources until it is completely terminated) even without my change, and the system needs to act as a whole to minimize that regardless of these temporary blips.

In practice, most production workloads take non-zero time to terminate after deletion.  The scheduler is eager - it tries to place immediately.  Because scheduler + kubelet form a distributed system where network requests can be arbitrarily delayed the kubelet could reject the incoming request because the scheduler is out of date.  The overall goal is to minimize those sorts of conflicts.

We could make the scheduler less eager, but that wouldn't necessarily fix scenarios where multiple schedulers are running and crucially, wouldn't make us more resilient to burst scenarios.  Reverting the change makes the node less resilient.  If we think about this as a race condition, that helps frame the problem more effectively:

> The kubelet has to address how to deal with pods that *could* run in the near future, but *can't* be started yet because the resources they need are not yet available.

Since deletion is one way, we know that eventually the terminating pods will finish.  However, we can't anticipate how long it will be before those pods can be started.  The admission rejection path today gives the scheduler an opportunity to place a pod on another node in some cases (rejecting the pod leads to a workload controller creating another one which might be able to go to another node).  This isn't guaranteed.

There are a couple of scenarios to consider:

1. Pods that want access to exclusive resources (isolated CPUs, PV slots on cloud systems, unique devices)
2. Nodes with a lot of churn (multiple pods starting and terminating)

In both of these cases we could imagine adding a new category of pod admission - pods that *could* run in the near future, once other terminating pods reach terminal state.  That ideally is an unordered list since Kubelets today do not guarantee that property (if a node restarts and has less memory than previously, the kubelet will reject pods semi-arbitrarily).  When checking for admission, we'd allow a pod to pass hard admission if the pod fits within that boundary (active + terminating), but we wouldn't allocate any resources for that pod or start it until those resources become free.

This would require some changes (potentially significant) to kubelet admission.  We'd need to split kubelet pod admission into a verification phase and a mutation phase (like apiserver) and admission plugins like cpu-manager (and others?) would have to be changed to accomodate.  Pods would get verified (can this pod run at all), then accepted (we think we can satisfy this request in the near future), then when we reach soft admission in the pod sync loop is when resources should be allocated (we can start this pod right now).  If an allocation fails, we'd have to be careful to clean it up (a set of partial allocations on stopped pods would be bad).  Likewise, if a pod is in soft admission too long we might simply want to terminate it (although we'd need to think about whether allowing it in creates a perception that it's safe to just wait for the end user).

In brief, that's:

* Pod hard admission has to block impossible requests (requesting 16 cores when we have 8 available)
* Pod hard admission has to allow some future possible requests (requesting 2 cores when we have 0 free but 2 will be released when pod p2 terminates) by taking into account terminating pods + active pods (if we have 8 available cores, 6 running, 0 waiting, and 2 terminating, we can accept 2 cores).  Pod hard admission MUST not accept more than 8 total cores.
* Pod soft admission has to be responsible for deciding whether an admitted but not yet started up can start (wait until there are currently 2 free cpus, then that pod can start)
* All "allocation" of resources should happen in soft admission, and it allocation fails the allocated resources need to be cleaned up inside the admission plugins within some time T 
    - this is a potentially racy situation of course, so it's probably better if admission plugins get passed the set of running pods by the cleanup loop vs doing it themselves (needs follow up)

We might frame this as pods pass between the following phases:

* `candidate` (pod has never been considered to run on the node but is now visible via the api or static pods)
   * tracked by the pod config loop
* `admitted` (it is possible to run this pod given the resource constraints defined, but may not be possible until some pods terminate)
   * gated by hard admission
   * tracked by the pod config loop
* `syncing` (any resources the pod needs are available and the pod can consume those resources)
   * gated by soft admission
   * tracked by the pod worker
* `terminating` (the pod is still running on the kubelet, so any resources it uses must be still accounted for by admission)
   * tracked by the pod worker
* `terminated` (the pod can be ignored from a resource consumption perspective)

Existing terms:

* `active pods` (pre 1.22, this meant "admitted pods that haven't started terminating" which was wrong, now it means admitted pods that have not terminated)
* `admitted pods` (should be any pod that has passed hard admission)

The bug today is that resources are being allocated in hard admission, and that the kubelet doesn't allow admission of a pod whose resources will be freed in the future due to a currently `terminating` pod.

That's ok.  Because that's *already* the case - the Kubelet owns the phase once `spec.nodeName` is set, not the apiserver.  There is always a race between the state the kubelet knows and the state that everyone else knows.

We can't introduce new phases at this point without taking a lot of risk we break significantly more workloads than we fix.  We could add conditions, but adding a new phase would break all the existing users who don't expect that phase to show up (in general we don't add enums to our api because the risk of breaking code that assumes the phase is limited to the original 5 will break).  Adding a condition wouldn't be enough either, but we could definitely add a condition someone uses BEFORE we transition the phase to indicate the pod is doing something (we'd just have to figure out whether that's useful).

As the comment notes, there is a contract in place today between the kubelet and the scheduler that already took this into account - the scheduler expects that terminal phase means "can schedule new pods that reuse exclusive resources as described by the resources and device lists".  The kubelet has  been incorrectly providing that contract the moment we added admission-controlled exclusive resources (for cpu and device manger) - we just didn't know that because we were not taking terminating containers into account on exclusivity.  Once we took terminating containers into account (less wrong), we discovered (here) that containers can be marked terminal in phase too early.
